newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Leclerc tank star of Bastille Day parade.
newsitem.headline: France's Leclerc tank star of Bastille Day parade.

text.p: France's new Leclerc tank was the undisputed star of the traditional Bastille Day march-past on Monday when 5,000 soldiers, 300 vehicles and 90 aircraft paraded on or over Paris' Champs Elysees avenue.

Some 27 Leclercs rolled down the broad avenue for the first time and a further 12 were driven aboard transport vehicles past conservative President Jacques Chirac and the left-wing cabinet who shared a reviewing stand on the Place de la Concorde.
GIAT-Industrie, state-owned makers of the 60-tonne Leclerc, describe it as the most advanced main battle tank in the world.
The army, which initially hoped for more than 800 Leclercs, has had to cut its order to 420 because of budget constraints. The United Arab Emirates have ordered 436 for $3.6 billion.
France also hopes to sell up to 300 Leclercs to Saudi Arabia which already has the earlier AMX-30 French tank in its ranks.
Critics say the Leclerc, first on the drawing board 20 years ago, is still not operational in the French army.
They also say state-of-the-art electronics have inflated the price tag for each tank to 28 million francs ($4.66 million).
Critics say the "real" unit cost to the state, including development costs, is about 80 million francs ($13 million) for a tank that may be too sophisticated for the battlefield.
Chirac said on Sunday he would make sure that the armed forces, anxious at possible budget cuts by a new left-wing government, received the resources they needed.
Thousands of onlookers, including many foreign tourists, lined the Champs Elysees in bright sunshine to watch the parade, one of the last such military displays in a major democracy.
The armoured units followed such traditional favourites as camouflage-clad, red bereted paratroopers and slow-stepping foreign legionnaires.

Chirac, who launched a landmark shift from conscription to all-professional armed forces last year, said he would review with the Socialist-led government what objectives had been met after the first year of a 1996 six-year military planning law.

"Today, we have made a good start...With the government, we are going to draw up a balance sheet of objectives achieved in this first year of implementation and the defence minister will send you the conclusions," he told senior commanders.
His comment appeared to be a warning shot across the bows of Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, who is looking for cost savings on defence.
Senior army officers were worried by the appointment of a tough budget expert, Socialist Alain Richard, with no military expertise, as defence minister last month.

Richard said in a radio interview that he would make a decision within two weeks about the future of the "citizens meetings" programme which the past centre-right government wished to introduce as the armed forces phased out conscription in favour of all-professional forces.
Socialist spokesmen have said that the "citizens meeting", a five-day programme of medical checks and civics lectures for all youths aged 19 or 20, was costly and useless.
In the southern France port of Toulon, a Bastille Day parade was marked by clashes between anti-racist militants and members of the extreme rightist National Front party.
